title: Central Ideas and Details
lead: These questions give you a short passage, from a work of literature or a scholarly text, and ask one of two things: “Which choice best states the main idea of the text?” or a specific question such as “According to the text, why did…?” They are the most direct reading questions on the test. You need no outside knowledge and no complicated reasoning, only careful reading. The answer is always in the passage.

parts.title: Part 1 · Two kinds of question
parts.html:
Central idea questions ask for the main idea of the whole passage. A main idea is a topic plus the point made about it. “Bees” is a topic. “Bees communicate food locations through dance” is an idea.

A correct main ideaA wrong main idea
Covers most of what the passage saysFixes on one detail and leaves out the rest
Includes whatever the passage stresses mostBrings in an idea the passage never mentions
Contradicts something in the passage

Detail questions ask about one specific piece of information. The answer usually sits in a single sentence, and the question contains words or phrases that point you to it.

parts.title: Part 2 · The four-step method
parts.html:
1. Summarize the text in your own words. Read closely; do not skim. By the end you should be able to say what the passage told you.
  2. Check the task. Does the question ask for the main idea, or for one particular piece of information?
  3. Go back to the text. For a main idea, look at your summary and find the thread that runs through all of it. For a detail, go to the sentence the question points to.
  4. Predict, then eliminate. Answer the question in your own words before you read the choices, then look for the match. If you are still unsure, cross out every choice that contradicts the passage or adds something new.

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example: main idea
parts.html:
Many intellectual histories of the Black Power movement of the 1960s and 1970s rely heavily on essays and other explicitly ideological works as primary sources, a tendency that can overrepresent the perspectives of a small number of thinkers, most of whom were male. Historian Ashley D. Farmer has shown that expanding the array of primary sources to encompass more types of print material—including political cartoons, advertisements, and artwork—leads to a much better understanding of the movement and the crucial and diverse roles that Black women played in shaping it. Which choice best describes the main idea of the text?
A) Before Farmer’s research, historians had largely ignored the intellectual dimensions of the Black Power movement.
B) Farmer’s methods and research have enriched the historical understanding of the Black Power movement and Black women’s contributions to it.
C) Other historians of the Black Power movement have criticized Farmer’s use of unconventional primary sources.
D) The figures in the Black Power movement whom historians tend to cite would have agreed with Farmer’s conclusions about women’s roles in the movement.

Summarize. Three points: most histories of the movement draw on a narrow set of sources and mostly on men; Farmer uses a wider range of sources; her approach gives a fuller picture, especially of what women did.

Predict. “Farmer’s wider sources improve our understanding of the movement and of women’s part in it.”

Test the choices.

  • A contradicts the passage, which opens with “many intellectual histories” that already existed.
  • C adds something new. The passage says nothing about how other historians reacted to Farmer.
  • D adds something new as well. The passage never says what the movement’s figures would have thought.
  • B matches the prediction, mentions women’s contributions, and adds nothing. It is the answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · Main idea: the size check
parts.html:
Wrong main-idea choices are usually the wrong size. Check each choice against your summary:

  • Too narrow: one supporting detail raised to the level of the main idea. Ask whether the whole passage serves this, or one sentence.
  • Too broad: covers something the passage only touches. Ask whether the passage develops it, or mentions it once.
  • True but not central: accurate and straight from the passage, but not what the passage is about. This is the most dangerous kind. On a main idea question, being true is not enough.

Watch the last sentence. Short SAT passages often save their point for the end, especially science passages, where the setup comes first and the significance last. If your summary ignores the final sentence, it is probably incomplete.

If you are torn between two choices, ask: if I crossed this idea out, what would the passage lose? The main idea is the thing the passage cannot lose.

parts.title: Part 5 · Details: use the keywords as a map
parts.html:
1. Find the keywords in the question, such as a name, a date or a term, and locate them in the passage. They lead you to the sentence that holds the answer.
  2. Read exactly what that sentence says, then match it to a choice. The danger is a choice that is almost the sentence, with one actor or condition swapped.
  3. Compare near-misses word by word. When two choices share the key terms, the difference is usually one small word: “most” vs. “some”, “caused” vs. “correlated with”, “juveniles” vs. “adults”, “prevented” vs. “reduced”.
Example. “The 1990s revival of vinyl records surprised industry analysts, though sales remained well below their 1970s peak, and the revival was driven largely by collectors under thirty.”
Wrong choiceWhat it changes
Vinyl sales in the 1990s exceeded their 1970s levelsReverses a fact
The revival was driven by industry marketing campaignsSwaps the actor: the text credits collectors
Analysts predicted the vinyl revivalSwaps the verb: they were surprised

The correct choice must keep all three facts, including “below their 1970s peak”, which weak choices often quietly drop.

Tip. Put your finger on the sentence that answers the question before you look at the choices. If you cannot point to it, you are answering from memory, and memory is where the trap choices live.

parts.title: Part 6 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Stay specificDo not go beyond what the passage covers. Reject choices that widen or blur its ideas, and watch for a small twist that makes a choice sound relevant while saying something the passage does not support.
Leave your own knowledge outIf you happen to know the topic, do not use what you know. A choice that is true in the real world but not stated in the passage is wrong.
Keep predictions shortA prediction as long as the passage is no use. Cut it down until it is one brief idea. The shorter it is, the faster you can test it against the choices.
Keywords as a mapOn detail questions, find the question’s key words in the passage and read around them.

The reading habits from Class 1 apply here too: strip the details, do not stall on a hard word, shorten the jargon, and eliminate before you guess.

parts.title: Part 7 · Topic, scope and “so what?”
parts.html:
Find the topic first. The topic is the person, thing or idea the text keeps coming back to. In a text this short it is named in the first sentence or straight after it, and then returns in other words: a telescope becomes “the instrument”, “the device”, “it”.

Check the scope: one or many? If the text is about one painter, a choice about “painters” is too broad, however accurate the rest of it is. The correct choice names the topic or a close rewording of it, and it is sometimes the only choice that does.

Topic + “so what?” = main point. A main point is not a topic (“coral reefs”) and not a theme (“survival”). It is what the text wants you to know about the topic.

Summarize the argument, not the content. Compare two ways of summing up the same text.

Gardeners have long been told that watering at midday scorches leaves, because the droplets act as tiny lenses. When plant scientists tested the idea on smooth-leaved plants, however, the droplets evaporated long before any damage appeared. Only on leaves covered in fine hairs, which hold droplets above the surface, did small burns form.
Kind of summaryWhat it sounds like
Content (too long)“It says gardeners think watering at noon burns leaves because of lenses, and then scientists tried it on smooth leaves and the drops dried up, but on hairy leaves…”
ArgumentMidday watering burns leaves only in a few cases.
Scratch-paper versionnoon water ≠ burn (only hairy leaves)

The second and third versions are what you need. They drop every detail and keep the one thing the text is there to say.

Old idea, new idea. Many science and social science texts have the same shape: what people used to believe, then what the evidence now shows. The main point is almost always the new idea.

Signals of the old ideaSignals of the new idea
have long believed, traditionally, for decades, it is commonly assumed, many people think, some researchers claimhowever, but, in fact, in reality, recent research shows, it now appears, a new study suggests

In the text above, “have long been told” announces the old idea, and “however” marks the turn. You can often predict the main point from the opening words alone: a text that begins “It was long assumed that…” is about to say the assumption was wrong. Jot the two ideas down (“old: noon water burns; new: mostly not”) so that you do not choose a choice that states the old one.

parts.title: Part 8 · Fiction and poetry
parts.html:
Literary texts do not make an argument, but the method changes very little.

  • Ask who is involved, what happens, and how they feel about it. That is the main idea of a fiction text.
  • Look at the beginning and the end. As in other texts, the important information tends to sit there, and the last sentence often shows the character's reaction.
  • Be literal. Do not hunt for symbols or a hidden message. Students lose points on these texts by interpreting too much, not too little. Use only what the words say.
  • For a poem, turn each sentence into plain prose before you look at the choices. The idea may be carried by an image, but the answer must still be supported by the wording.
  • For “overall structure”, state what happens and how the character reacts, then test the last part of each choice first.
Example. Mira had practised the speech for a week, timing herself against the kitchen clock. Now, with the hall full and her name already announced, she found that every sentence had left her. She looked at the front row, saw her grandmother nodding as if the speech had already begun, and started to talk about the garden instead.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text? A) A character regrets that she did not prepare for an important event.
B) A character who loses her prepared words finds another way to begin, encouraged by a relative.
C) A character is pressured by her family into speaking in public.
D) Speaking in public is frightening for most people. Who, what, how: Mira forgets her speech, sees her grandmother, and starts on a different subject.
A is contradicted (she practised for a week). C is not in the text. D is too broad: the text is about one person.
B covers the beginning, the turn and the end.

parts.title: Part 9 · Pronouns and summary nouns
parts.html:
Writers avoid repeating a long idea by packing it into a pronoun (it, they, this) or a general noun: this finding, this shift, such concerns, the process, the claim. Hard questions often depend on knowing exactly what one of these words points to, and choices use the same kind of general noun.

The rule: go back. The idea being pointed to is nearly always before the word, often a full sentence before. Reading on in the hope that it becomes clear does not work, and neither does rereading the phrase alone.

Glass frogs sleep on green leaves, and while they sleep they draw most of their red blood cells into the liver. This retreat makes their bodies two to three times more transparent, hiding them from predators. “This retreat” = drawing the red blood cells into the liver
A question could ask why the frogs become harder to see. The answer is that idea, not the word “retreat”.
  • Singular or plural. “It” needs a singular noun and “they” a plural one. When two nouns are possible, the number usually decides.
  • The same pronoun can change its target. “It” in one sentence and “it” in the next may refer to different things. Check each one.
  • The former, the latter. “The former” is the first of two things just mentioned, and “the latter” is the second. “Granite and sandstone were both quarried nearby; the former was used for bridges, the latter for houses.” Bridges: granite. Houses: sandstone.

Tip. If a sentence starts with “this”, “these” or “such” and you cannot say in a few words what it refers to, you have not understood the sentence yet. Go back before going on.
